drills.q: A stage's task duration histogram shows 199 tasks at ~4 seconds and 1 task at 38 minutes. What's your first diagnostic step, and what would confirm it's skew rather than a hardware issue?
drills.a: Check that outlier task's shuffle-read size in the Spark UI. If it's a large multiple of the median shuffle-read size across sibling tasks, it's data skew (one key dominating a hash-partitioned shuffle). A hardware/slow-node issue would instead show normal data volume with abnormally slow processing per byte, and typically GC or scheduler-delay metrics standing out instead.

drills.q: Your job has AQE enabled with default settings and still shows classic skew symptoms on a sort-merge join. List the two threshold conditions AQE's skew-join feature requires, and give a scenario where both pass but skew handling still doesn't apply.
drills.a: Both spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.skewedPartitionFactor (default 5x the median partition size) AND spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.skewedPartitionThresholdInBytes (default 256MB) must be exceeded. Even if both thresholds are cleared, skew handling only applies to sort-merge joins — if this is actually a groupBy aggregation or a non-equi join, AQE's skew-join feature doesn't engage at all regardless of thresholds.

drills.q: Write the salting pattern for a skewed groupBy aggregation (sum by key) that AQE cannot fix, and explain why it requires two groupBy stages instead of one.
drills.a: salted = df.withColumn('salt', (F.rand()*N).cast('int')); partial = salted.groupBy('key','salt').agg(F.sum('value').alias('p')); final = partial.groupBy('key').agg(F.sum('p').alias('total')). Two stages are needed because the first groupBy spreads the hot key's rows across N salted sub-keys (each landing on a different partition, breaking the skew), producing N partial sums per original key; the second groupBy combines those N partial sums back into one true total per key — a single groupBy on the salted key alone would leave the results incorrectly split by salt value.

drills.q: A join between a 5GB fact table and what you believe is a 50MB dimension table runs as a sort-merge join, not a broadcast. Diagnose two possible causes and how you'd verify each.
drills.a: 1) Table statistics are stale or were never computed, so the optimizer's size estimate for the dimension table exceeds autoBroadcastJoinThreshold (10MB default) even though the real size is 50MB over that but the estimate might be far higher; check with explain(mode='cost') and compare against ANALYZE TABLE output. 2) autoBroadcastJoinThreshold itself is still at the 10MB default and 50MB genuinely exceeds it; check the configured value and consider raising it (with fresh statistics) or adding an explicit .hint('broadcast').

drills.q: You convert a slow @udf(...) function to a @pandas_udf and get only a 1.5x speedup instead of the expected 10x+. What kind of UDF logic would explain a small gain like this?
drills.a: Logic that doesn't vectorize well — e.g. a UDF that calls an external network API per row, does row-dependent sequential computation, or branches heavily per element in a way that can't be expressed as NumPy/pandas vector operations. The pandas UDF still reduces JVM<->Python transfer overhead via Arrow batching, but if the actual per-row work itself can't be batched (each row still requires its own external call or scalar Python loop inside the pandas UDF), most of the win from vectorization is unavailable, leaving only the serialization-overhead reduction.

drills.q: An executor OOMs during a broadcast join, but Spark UI shows plenty of spill capacity was never used. Why didn't spill save it?
drills.a: The broadcast build side is materialized fully in memory by design — building and holding the broadcast variable isn't an operator that supports spilling to disk (unlike sort or shuffle-based aggregation). If the 'small' side turns out larger than the size estimate assumed, there's no fallback path; it's a hard OOM rather than a graceful disk-backed degradation.

drills.q: Explain, in terms of the Unified Memory Manager, how heavy caching on one part of a job can cause spill or slowdown on an unrelated concurrent operation in the same job.
drills.a: Cached data occupies storage memory within the Unified Memory region (bounded by memory.fraction of the heap, split by storageFraction between storage and execution as a soft boundary). Execution memory (needed for a concurrent large sort, aggregation, or hash-join build) can reclaim space from storage under pressure, but if the cache is large and actively pinned/reused, contention increases and the execution-hungry operator is more likely to be forced into disk spill than it would be without the concurrent cache pressure — the cache didn't directly cause the OOM/spill, but it shifted the effective available execution memory for everything else running at the same time.

drills.q: Design a bucketing scheme for two tables (orders, 2TB, and customers, 200GB) that are joined on customer_id in a nightly job that runs the same join pattern for the next year. Justify the bucket count and the risk if either table's write path changes.
drills.a: Bucket both tables by customer_id with the same bucket count, e.g. bucketBy(200, 'customer_id') sized so each bucket lands in a reasonable target size (roughly 2TB/200 = 10GB and 200GB/200 = 1GB per bucket, well within a single task's comfortable working set). This lets every nightly join skip the shuffle+sort entirely since both sides are pre-partitioned identically. Risk: if a future write to either table uses a different bucket count or a different write path that doesn't preserve bucketing (e.g. an ad hoc overwrite via a tool that ignores bucket metadata), the join silently falls back to a full shuffle join with no error, just a slower job — this needs to be caught by monitoring the job's plan (explain()) for the loss of the bucketed-join physical operator, not assumed to persist forever.

drills.q: A principal engineer asks you to justify, with the actual mechanism, why 'just throw more executors at it' is often the wrong first response to a slow Spark job. Give the mechanistic argument, not just 'sometimes it doesn't help.'
drills.a: Adding executors increases available parallel task slots, which only helps if the job's actual critical path is bounded by insufficient parallelism across many roughly-equal-sized tasks. If the critical path is instead one oversized skewed task (bounded by that single task's data volume on one core), a serial bottleneck (driver-side collect, one broadcast build, few output partitions), or a per-row Python UDF's CPU-bound interpreter overhead (bounded by per-core throughput, not core count), then idle additional executors simply wait alongside the existing ones for the same bottleneck to clear — the job's wall-clock time is set by its longest dependency chain, not by aggregate cluster capacity, and Amdahl's-law-style serial/skewed portions dominate exactly when scaling out stops helping.

drills.q: Contrast pandas UDFs and Arrow UDFs precisely: what conversion step does the Arrow UDF skip, and what's the measured tradeoff?
drills.a: A pandas UDF receives Arrow-batched data but Spark converts it into a pandas Series/DataFrame (and underlying NumPy arrays) before handing it to the user function, and converts the result back to Arrow after. An Arrow UDF operates directly on the Arrow columnar batch without that pandas/NumPy materialization step. Measured tradeoff: Arrow UDFs are reported roughly 10% faster and use about 40% less memory than pandas UDFs, with better native support for complex/nested types, at the cost of writing against the lower-level Arrow API instead of the more familiar pandas API.
